podcast.title: 39th Birthday Party in Munich (1985)
podcast.body: Freddie Mercury's 39th birthday celebration in Munich in 1985 is considered one of the two greatest parties in rock history. He invited all his friends to a costume party, and the images from this event, including guests arriving in horse-drawn carriages and the extravagant costumes, are iconic. It is often compared to Grace Jones's party at Studio 54 where Mick Jagger ended up hospitalized. "La grandísima fiesta de cumpleaños quiso Freddy Mercury en 1985. Son las dos mayores fiestas de la historia de Rock."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: QUEEN como iconografía estética y gráfica

podcast.title: Live Aid (1985) Iconic Outfit
podcast.body: Freddie Mercury's outfit at the Live Aid concert in 1985, consisting of white trousers with a red stripe and a yellow military-style jacket, has become an iconic piece of rock fashion. This look has been reinterpreted and referenced by various designers, such as Yves Saint Laurent and Martin Margiela, over the past 30 years. "El propio Freddy Mercury en el concierto de Life Aid, desde el pantalón Blanco con una banda roja hasta la cazadora Casa Cada Marilla que han sido versionados por distintos diseñadores como Isalora Go Martin Margel en los últimos 30 años."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: QUEEN como iconografía estética y gráfica

podcast.title: "I'm Going Slightly Mad" Music Video Outfit
podcast.body: In the music video for "I'm Going Slightly Mad," Freddie Mercury famously appears in a memorable aesthetic moment, portraying a version of the protagonist from "The Rocky Horror Picture Show" and notably wearing a banana wig. "Nos dejó uno de esos momentos apatióicos en los que Freddy Mercury se pone, una peluca de plátanos que es uno de esos momentos maravillosos de la iconografía de Queen."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: QUEEN como iconografía estética y gráfica

podcast.title: AIDS Complications
podcast.body: During the late stages of his battle with AIDS, Queen singer Freddie Mercury lost most of one of his feet due to complications from the disease. "he lost most of one of his feet to complications from the disease."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 60 Mind Blowing Facts in 60 Minutes: The 5th Edition

podcast.title: Creative Leader Archetype
podcast.body: Freddy Mercury is cited as an archetypal creative leader within a band, entirely focused on the artistic output. This contrasts with "political leaders" who manage the band's business and strategic decisions. "líderes que han ocupado un rol muy creativo como puede ser el caso de Freddy Mercury en Queen, que era el líder azulamente creativo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Wu-Tang Clan como Negocio Musical

podcast.title: Flash Gordon Era Outfit
podcast.body: During the "Flash Gordon" era, Freddie Mercury sported one of his most iconic looks, featuring a Flash Gordon t-shirt with contrasting borders, leather shorts, and was famously photographed standing atop a Darth Vader figure. This image is considered one of the coolest superhero-themed outfits and moments in rock history. "Ese momento de Freddy Mercury subido encima de Darth Vader es como lo más."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: QUEEN como iconografía estética y gráfica

podcast.title: Glam Rock Flamboyance
podcast.body: Freddie Mercury's flamboyance as frontman for Queen is recognized as a clear example of glam rock's influence on showmanship and visual style. "Freddie Mercury's Flamboyance with Queen, glam rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Posthumous Impact on AIDS Awareness
podcast.body: The only positive outcome of Freddie Mercury's death was the immense social commotion it caused, which arguably made it the most impactful AIDS-related death globally. It significantly helped change the perception of the disease among more conservative people, greatly contributing to awareness and visibility for those suffering from AIDS. "yo creo que con diferencia fue la muerte por sida que más conmozino al mundo y yo creo que ayudó muchísimo a cambiar la concepción que tenía mucha gente más conservadora sobre esta enfermedad."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Artistas gays que cambiaron nuestra sociedad.

podcast.title: Primary Songwriting Instrument
podcast.body: Freddie Mercury wrote much of Queen's greatest songs on the piano. His use of the instrument was fundamental to the band's iconic sound and compositions, highlighting its central role in their creative process. "Freddie Mercury of Queen wrote much of their greatest songs on piano."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Piano Heroes

podcast.title: Proud Life and Public Harassment Before AIDS Death
podcast.body: Throughout his life, Freddie Mercury proudly defended his way of living, full of parties and debauchery, never feeling uncomfortable or ashamed, emphasizing it was the life he enjoyed and that made him happy, independent of stereotypes. Tragically, he fell ill with AIDS, and British society's response was severely lacking. His diagnosis only became public two or three days before his death, after a year of intense harassment, including false blood tests confirming his illness. "Durante toda su vida, Freddie Mercury ha hecho una gran defensa de esa manera que le entendía de vivir la vida, de fiestas, de pasarlo bien, de libertinaje, nunca se sintió incomodado ni haber gonzado por la vida que llevaba y que le gustaba y que la llevó siempre con mucho orgullo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Artistas gays que cambiaron nuestra sociedad.

podcast.title: Queen II Cover Inspiration
podcast.body: Freddie Mercury was so captivated by the cover of Queen's second album that he became infatuated with recreating its image on video. This strong visual desire directly fueled the concept and production of the groundbreaking "Bohemian Rhapsody" music video. "Freddie Mercury started it all when he became infatuated with the cover of Queen's second album and wanted to create that image on video."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1

podcast.title: Queen Logo Designer
podcast.body: Freddie Mercury, known for his vocal talent, was also a skilled draftsman who studied plastic arts. He is credited with designing the core structure of the iconic Queen logo. "Freddy Mercury aparte de un gran cantante era un gran dibujante de hecho estudiar desplásticas."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: QUEEN como iconografía estética y gráfica

podcast.title: Tragic End and Societal Stigma
podcast.body: Despite living in an advanced society, Freddie Mercury could not achieve his wish to die peacefully and without stigma among his loved ones. He died reclusive, embroiled in scandal, and pointed out by many, simply for having the misfortune of contracting a disease that was killing thousands. "o sea tuvo que morir, recluido, inmersen el escándalo, señalado por todos, simplemente por haber tenido la mala suerte de tener una enfermedad que estaba matando a miles de personas."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

xref.title: "Today" Show Interview (1976) – National Controversy
xref.body: On Wednesday, December 1st, 1976, the Sex Pistols appeared on the popular UK tea-time chat show *Today*, hosted by Bill Grundy. They were a last-minute replacement for Queen, who had to cancel due to Freddie Mercury's throat infection. The band and their entourage consumed a bottle of Blue Nun in the limo and more liquor in the green room before going on live, unaware the show was unedited. Grundy's provocative questioning led to the band using profanity on air, which resulted in Grundy's two-week suspension, the producer and director's firing, and widespread media outrage with headlines like "the filth and the fury." This 117-second incident, despite being accidental, massively boosted punk rock's profile in the UK, causing "Anarchy in the UK" sales to jump from 10,000 copies in a week to 10,000 copies a day. "The impact of that 117 second interview was immediate."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 10

xref.title: Canceled "Today" Show Appearance (1976)
xref.body: Queen was originally booked as the guest for the "Today" chat show on December 1, 1976, but had to cancel because singer Freddie Mercury needed a trip to the dentist. Their marketing team suggested the Sex Pistols as a replacement. "The original guests were supposed to be another new group called Queen, but their singer, guy named Freddie Mercury, needed a trip to the dentist so they were forced to cancel."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 4

xref.title: Cancelled "Today" Show Appearance (1976)
xref.body: Queen was scheduled to appear on the popular UK chat show *Today* on December 1st, 1976, as part of their pre-release press tour for *A Day at the Races*. However, singer Freddie Mercury "suddenly took ill" with a throat infection, forcing the band to cancel their live appearance. This cancellation opened the slot for the Sex Pistols, leading to their infamous, career-defining interview. "But singer Freddie Mercury suddenly took ill. It was a throat infection or something. And Queen, the band, had to cancel their appearance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 10

xref.title: Cancelled TV Appearance (December 1, 1976)
xref.body: Queen was scheduled to be a guest on Bill Grundy's "Today" talk show on ITV on December 1, 1976. However, they had to cancel at the last minute, reportedly because Freddie Mercury needed to be rushed to the dentist for a bad toothache. Their cancellation led to the Sex Pistols being invited as a last-minute replacement. "But at the last second they had to cancel. Everybody seems to recall it was because somebody in the band needed to be rushed to the dentist with a bad toothache. I think it was Freddie Mercury."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Why Punk Happened

xref.title: Infamous "Today" TV Appearance (1976) - National Scandal
xref.body: On December 1, 1976, the Sex Pistols were booked as last-minute substitute guests on the bland "Today" chat show after Queen cancelled due to Freddie Mercury needing a dentist. Lured to the studio with champagne and beer, the band members were "heavily toasted" upon arrival. The two-minute interview, which featured multiple instances of swearing on live television, including the word "f**k," immediately became a gigantic national scandal, leading to headlines condemning "punk rock scum" and "the filth in the fury." "This two minutes has gone down in history as one of the most legendary rock and roll television appearances ever."

xref.title: Disapproval of "Bohemian Rhapsody" Cover
xref.body: Robert Plant expressed strong disapproval when The Trews performed a "punky version" of Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" during their shared tour, especially after it earned them a standing ovation. He conveyed his feelings by stating he knew Freddie Mercury and felt it was inappropriate to "relive the past," even directly accosting their drummer Sean about it. "He didn't want us doing that anymore... he told us it was because he knew Freddie and we're not here to relive the past."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words

xref.title: Exceptional Vocal Range
xref.body: Axl Rose possesses an exceptionally wide vocal range, which is noted to be greater than that of Freddie Mercury, Prince, and Mariah Carey. He is capable of hitting notes spanning over five and a half octaves. "Axel Rose has a wide vocal range, wider than Freddie Mercury prints and even Mariah Kerry. Axel Rose can hit notes over five and a half octaves."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Freddie Mercury's Love for Cats
xref.body: Freddie Mercury was famously devoted to his cats, going so far as to call home from the road to speak with them. "Freddie Mercury, who is nuts about his cats, golf and phone home from the road, just to talk to them. Seriously."

xref.title: Initial Public Reaction and Intent
xref.body: Upon the release of The Darkness's debut album *Permission to Land* in 2003, there was an initial public reaction questioning if the band, and Justin Hawkins's vocal style, was a joke or a parody of Freddie Mercury and Queen. However, Hawkins maintained that his approach was, and remains, entirely serious. His use of high-pitched vocals was noteworthy because it had been a long time since such a style was prevalent in Alt Rock. "This guy's making fun of Freddie Mercury or Queen. No, Justin was and remains dead serious."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Taylor Hawkins' All-Time Favorite Band
xref.body: Queen held a special place as Taylor Hawkins' all-time favorite band. He greatly admired their music and often dared to tackle Freddie Mercury's vocal parts when he would step out from behind the drum kit to sing for the Foo Fighters. "Queen was his all time favorite band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: The "Bohemian Rhapsody" Incident
xref.body: During their tour with Robert Plant, a fan dared The Trews on live radio to perform their old cover of Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" at a sold-out show in Rexall Place, Edmonton. The band delivered a "punky version" that garnered a standing ovation. This angered Robert Plant, who, having known Freddie Mercury, didn't want the past relived. He "accosted" their drummer, Sean, the next day in Calgary, but later issued a public apology by praising Canadian songwriters, including The Trews, at the Saddledome. "we got word that we really ticked Robert Plant off."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Trews: In Their Own Words
